newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels promise cooperation with aid agencies.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels promise cooperation with aid agencies.

text.p: Zairian rebels promised Friday to cooperate with U.N. aid agencies as an airlift to repatriate up to 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees from northeastern Zaire gathered pace.

Moise Nyarugabo, a senior official in the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL), told a news conference aid agencies would be allowed more access to refugee camps south of Kisangani and could also use a railway.
But he also railed against what he called U.N. inefficiency in dealing with the refugee crisis in the last two weeks.
"We have had complaints and accusations that we are not allowing them to do their job, but they are not doing their job," said Nyarugabo. "It is up to them to show they can do it."
The U.N. refugee agency flew 781 refugees out of Kisangani city on four flights Friday, bringing the total since the airlift began Sunday to 2,583, a UNHCR spokesman said.
The refugees, who are members of Rwanda's Hutu majority, fled their homeland in 1994 and the country's minority Tutsis collectively accuse them of genocide in Rwanda the same year.
Paul Stromberg, UNHCR spokesman in Kisangani, said four flights took refugees to Rwanda Friday but a plane was unable to carry 300 refugee children home because of fuel shortages.
He said a transit center in Kisangani was almost empty but thousands of refugees were expected by train later Friday.

Aid officials have complained that despite rebel leader Laurent Kabila's promise to allow them free access to Biaro camp, 25 miles south of Kisangani, they have been restricted to less than three hours a day there since Monday.
Monday was the first day in a week that aid workers were allowed to visit Biaro and Kasese camps, which emptied after bloody clashes between villagers, rebel soldiers and refugees.
Nyarugabo strongly denied rebel soldiers were involved in the attacks on the camps despite witness reports from refugees.
But he said in answer to a question about reports of fights between rebels in Goma city in eastern Zaire: "If individual (rebels) make a mistake you can't say there is a problem with the whole army."
More than 80,000 refugees at Biaro and Kasese fled into the dense forest. Aid officials say hundreds of them may have died.
Conditions at Biaro, where a cholera outbreak last month delayed the start of an airlift, have worsened since the exodus.
More than 30,000 refugees have returned to the camp this week but are living in appalling conditions with no clean water, little medical attention and food and hardly any shelter.
Many have terrible wounds -- caused by machetes, axes and bullets -- and the number of unaccompanied children has soared.
Annick Jeantet, a coordinator with the U.N. Children's Fund UNICEF, said six childen died overnight of disease or injury.
Local Red Cross workers said they had buried more than 200 people since they returned to the camp Monday. Refugees say hundreds of corpses are strewn through the surrounding forest.

U.N. agencies said Friday rebels who abducted 52 sick Hutu refugee children from a hospital had kept them in a container van without food or water and beat some of them before releasing them five days later.
UNHCR said it had asked the Tutsi-dominated rebels, who face mounting charges of alleged human rights abuses and violence against the refugees, to explain the abduction and mistreatment.
Rebels released the children Wednesday in the eastern city of Bukavu after a U.N. protest and they were repatriated.
